abstract: The interfacial organization of synovial fluid (SF) contributes to cartilage protection and lubrication, yet how articular cartilage extracellular matrix (AC-ECM) identity influences the rheological response of supramolecularly assembled SF films remains to be elucidated. Here, depth-resolved multiple-particle tracking microrheology was used to examine diluted SF (dSF) near immobilized collagen type II (Col-II), collagen type I (Col-I), and fibronectin (FN). Untreated dSF exhibited increased relative apparent viscosity near Col-II and FN, whereas the response near Col-I was comparatively negligible. Treatment with StcE, a mucin-selective protease previously shown to cleave lubricin's mucin domain in SF, resulted in more pronounced effects of the interface on the depth dependent viscosity profiles across all three substrates. Analysis of the complex modulus and viscosity revealed significant effects with depth changes and StcE treatment. Quartz crystal microbalance measurements further revealed that the adsorbed amount of the fluids onto AC-ECM substrates did not directly correspond to the magnitude of microrheological modulation, with Col-I showing limited retention despite a pronounced near-interface response following StcE treatment. Together, these findings indicate that AC-ECM identity and StcE-sensitive SF constituents are associated with spatial variations in viscoelasticity that are not directly reflected by far-field tracer dynamics or interfacial adsorption alone.
